extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application’s specification, drawings, and original claims satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph), including when amendments, priority/continuation claims, range changes, genus/species claims, and alleged new matter raise issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim must be described in the application as filed in a manner that shows the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention; the claim need not be described literally using the same terms as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure/addition/deletion) should be concluded by the examiner as not described in the application, resulting in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) or denial of benefit of an earlier filing date. See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical situations raising written description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues commonly arise in specific procedural contexts where it must be determined whether the claim subject matter is supported in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical contexts include: (I) amendments affecting a claim (including specification amendments that indirectly affect claims); (II) claiming the benefit of an earlier U.S. filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120; (III) relying on foreign or provisional priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)/(e); and (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference. Each circumstance requires assessing whether the earlier or original disclosure meets the 35 U.S.C. 112(a) written description standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption and burden on examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification as filed is strongly presumed adequate to satisfy written description unless and until the examiner rebuts the presumption with sufficient evidence or reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims. The inquiry is case-by-case and is a question of fact. See In re Wertheim, In re Marzocchi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements (what examiner must state)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting claims for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the original disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. In some cases a simple, specific statement pointing out the lack of apparent support may be sufficient, particularly for new or amended claims where applicant has not indicated support. When appropriate, suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the original disclosure but avoid adding new matter. See Hyatt v. Dudas; Rasmussen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to applicant's reply — reexamination before repeating rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Before repeating a written description rejection after applicant's reply, the examiner must review the record as a whole including amendments, arguments, and submitted evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record demonstrates that the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection in the next Office action. If the record still does not demonstrate adequacy, the rejection may be repeated, the examiner must fully respond to applicant’s rebuttal, and must thoroughly analyze and discuss any affidavits or evidence submitted in the reply (see In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to claim scope — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common problematic changes include broadening or narrowing claim breadth, altering numerical range limitations, or using terminology not synonymous with the original disclosure. See MPEP § 2163 for guidelines and case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claims — omission of a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting a limitation originally disclosed can raise written description issues when it causes the claim to cover a broader invention than what the inventor demonstrated possession of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the omitted element was described as essential or critical in the original disclosure, the broadened claim may fail the written description (and possibly enablement) requirement. Case examples: Gentry Gallery (control means location essential), Tronzo (generic cup vs conical cup), In re Wilder. Compare In re Peters where a removed shape limitation was not essential. If the specification describes an element as essential, omitting it from a claim typically does not comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claims — adding a generic (genus) claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by sufficient description of a representative number of species; one species may suffice only in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'representative number of species' means the adequately described species reflect the variation within the genus. Where there is substantial variation, one must describe enough species to reflect that variation. Disclosure of a single species supports a genus only if it indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. If the disclosure teaches against other species or artisans could not predict operability beyond the disclosed species, genus claims may lack support. Cases: Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis, In re Rasmussen, Tronzo, In re Gosteli. Functional recitations of known compounds may sometimes be sufficient (In re Herschler; In re Smythe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing narrower or subgenus limitations not supported by the original disclosure can violate written description; whether subgeneric language is acceptable is case-dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not necessarily provide written description of each species. Recitation of an undisclosed species may violate the requirement. Some subgeneric recitations are acceptable when species falling within the subgenus are disclosed; others are not. Each case must be decided on the facts as to what is reasonably communicated to those skilled in the art. Cases: Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson, In re Smith, In re Wilder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitations (numerical ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to numerical range limitations require analysis of what ranges a skilled artisan would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the original description reasonably conveys possession of the new range. Example: In re Wertheim — original disclosure of 25%-60% and examples of 36% and 50% did not support a new 'at least 35%' claim (because it opened to embodiments outside 25%-60%), but a limitation to 'between 35% and 60%' did meet the description requirement. Other cases (Purdue Pharma, Union Oil) illustrate that sufficiency depends on whether the disclosure conveys that the inventor considered the claimed range part of the invention and whether sufficient description shows possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description to new matter (statutory prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding content to the abstract, specification, drawings, or claims that was not described in the application as filed raises new matter issues; new matter is prohibited by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 prohibits introducing new matter into the disclosure; 35 U.S.C. 251 prohibits introducing new matter into a reissue application. If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require cancellation of the new matter. If new matter is added to the claims, the examiner should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph). See In re Rasmussen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and review of new matter objections/rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural handling differs: objections to added disclosure vs rejections of claims for new matter have different review routes and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An objection/requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181; a rejection of claims for new matter is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. If both objection and rejection exist (claims and specification contain new matter), the combined issue is appealable rather than petitionable. When claims are not amended but the specification is amended to add new matter, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) should be made whenever any claim limitation is affected by the added material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure — remedying lack of antecedent support
rubrics_metrics.description: Material originally claimed but not described in the remainder of the specification can be remedied by amending the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims filed in the original specification are part of the disclosure; thus if the original specification contains a claim that discloses material not disclosed elsewhere in the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include that claimed subject matter. Form paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. See In re Benno.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter (permitted changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rephrasing, correction of obvious errors, and inclusion of recognized definitions known at filing may be permissible and do not constitute new matter when they do not introduce new technical content beyond what was originally disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere rephrasing that preserves the same meaning is permissible (In re Anderson). Inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at filing may be acceptable, but if multiple definitions exist and one is chosen later, it must be clear from the original filing that applicant intended that definition (Scarring Corp. v. Megan). Correcting an obvious error is not new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize both the error and the appropriate correction (In re Odd). However, applicant generally may not rely on foreign priority documents to support correction of errors in a U.S. application unless the foreign document is explicitly incorporated by reference. For certain post‑2004 situations where portions were inadvertently omitted from the U.S. filing, 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.57(a) may permit incorporation by reference of the prior foreign filing under specified conditions. See MPEP § 217 and related CFR provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should suggest amendments when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a rejection is based on lack of written description, examiners should suggest claim amendments that can be supported by the original disclosure, mindful not to introduce new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application’s written description, being mindful of the prohibition against the addition of new matter in the claims or description. See Rasmussen.
